newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: New twist in Serbia election fraud, pressures mount.
newsitem.headline: New twist in Serbia election fraud, pressures mount.

text.p: The Serbian government added a new twist to legal battles over annulment of November municipal elections while Western countries warned that time was running out to restore the opposition victories.

The government said on Tuesday that a Justice Ministry inquiry had found no fraud in eight of 14 disputed local elections, a disclosure that may have boosted the cause of the opposition which has been demonstrating daily for nine weeks.

Officials of the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition were divided on how to interpret the ruling, which did not apply to the opposition's annulled victory in Belgrade, and Western diplomats said the situation remained confused.

One Western diplomat, speaking before the latest decision was announced, said the legal fight over the election results was so complex that people saw it as just a delaying tactic by socialist President Slobodan Milosevic.
"People get so fed up with the evidence of his ability to manipulate the system that the idea that they can change anything by going out on the streets is gone," the diplomat said.
In Washington, the State Department said it was "extremely disturbed" by the Serbian government's handling of the election dispute and accused Belgrade of tying up the issue in legal knots.
"They are now tying up this question of respect for elections in a judicial process that cannot be considered to be democratic by any means," spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said in Geneva that the Serbian government should move quickly to end the impasse and avoid an escalation of the opposition protests.

"If progress -- reinstatement -- is not made in this direction rapidly, an intensification of demonstrations awaits us -- a blockage of roads that could thus prevent normal economic life," Dini told a news conference.
"An escalation of conflict should be avoided," added Dini, who held talks with Zajedno leaders in Rome last weekend.

Former Spanish prime minister Felipe Gonzalez, who headed last month's OSCE mission to Belgrade which verified the opposition victories, said in Rome the election results had to be reinstated and there could be no "alternative formulas".
French rightist Jean-Marie Le Pen, invited to Belgrade by the ultra-nationalist Serbian Radical Party (SRS), also sided with the protesters.
"It appears to me that what is dividing this country is the communist dictatorship by President Milosevic," the leader of the anti-immigrant National Front said at a news conference.

The announcement of the results of the Justice Ministry's inquiry appeared to undercut the Socialist Party's case for having nullified the elections. But Zajedno legal advisers were divided on its significance.
"In this statement the government has in the clearest terms said that the Zajedno coalition absolutely won in those eight municipalities," said Goran Draganic, a Zajedno lawyer.
Milan Bozic, political adviser to Zajedno co-leader Vuk Draskovic, said the government had in fact rejected the findings of the Gonzalez mission and was just trying to buy time.
The Western diplomat said Milosevic's room for manoeuvre seemed to be vanishing.
"His (Milosevic's) control here is based on control of the bureaucracy, control of the party and control of state enterprises," the diplomat said.
"If he loses Belgrade and some of the other major cities then his ability to take care of his party is weakened."

The diplomat said legal wrangling could delay constitution of the municipal councils so long that Milosevic would appoint interim boards and hold new elections, which the opposition might well boycott.
"Then the question is can he get people to accept an authoritarian dictatorship in the heart of Europe and work with them?" the diplomat said.

"Or does he get so isolated that he literally has to choose between caving or going the direction of (Romania's late dictator Nicolae) Ceasescu -- impoverishing the country in the interest of maintaining his own authoritarian power."
